items.question: How do you think about the possibility of models thinking longer without verbalizing their reasoning?
items.object: Nonverbal reasoning and complementary ways of scaling thinking in humans and models
items.answer: I think it's clear that we can sometimes think longer about a problem without actually verbalizing the answer in our head. We don't always think in steps in our head, but even as humans we have these two ways in which we can scale compute or thinking in this way. I think that's kind of interesting. It's not necessarily you can do this or the other, but maybe as humans we naturally do both of those, and these models also could do both.

items.question: Why did you find the 2021 work on recurrent models that solve mazes motivating?
items.object: Recurrent models trained to solve mazes in 2021
items.answer:
The backstory to this whole recurrent approach is that way back when, some good colleagues of mine trained these models in 2021. We trained these recurrent models to solve mazes. It's really a toy problem, but it's kind of a very intriguing algorithmic task, because you train these small recurrent models on mazes of sizes like 13 by 13. It's a tiny pixelized maze. You look at it, and it's trivial what the solution is. You train these models on these 13 by 13 mazes, and then at test time you just run them for more recurrences, so you put in more compute. At test time you can solve arbitrarily large mazes. They have these funny pictures in the paper where the whole screen is filled, every pixel is a different pixel in this maze. It's an 8,000 by 8,000 pixel maze, and the model just puts in a lot of compute and solves it. It's an interesting example because this model really has learned the algorithm to solve mazes, or solve this particular kind of maze. I think that was also very motivating to see that you could really learn an algorithm like that.

But it was always a bit restricted, too. You could only learn mazes, or addition, or chess problems. These are all a bit of toy tasks, or very limited domains where we could see that these approaches would scale.

items.question: What do you find algorithmically interesting about recurrence in model depth?
items.object: Recurrence in model depth
items.answer: What's interesting here about recurrency, or how that comes in, is that people are very familiar with recurrent neural networks. In a recurrent neural network, what you have is a sequence, and the recurrence is basically that every time you go forward in the sequence, you do another step of computation. This is an efficient way to compute things about sequences. What we're doing here is a bit different: we're doing a recurrence in the depth of the model. A good analogy is that the model doesn't have a fixed amount of layers, but it has a small number of layers that it repeats. This relates to lots of approaches in that field, like weight sharing, sometimes called weight tying. In this way the model really has an arbitrary number of layers, which means that in comparison to our recurrent neural network, where you always produce more input or more output to do more compute, in a transformer, every time you want to do more compute, you have to produce more outputs. With this sort of recurrent depth, you can produce an arbitrary amount of compute before you compute the next output. The compute axis is disentangled from the output axis, from the context of the model, and that's what's so interesting algorithmically about this kind of approach.

items.question: How would you explain recurrent-depth computation in language models through an analogy with an RNN?
items.object: An RNN analogy for recurrent-depth computation
items.answer: I think the analogy for an RNN would be that you actually don't move to the next token in the sequence, but you produce filler outputs and then keep iterating on these filler outputs. That would be where you really stop on the sequence, where you currently stopped, keep on recurring a bit, and then you move forward.
quotes: For example, I think the analogy for an RNN would be that you actually don't move to the next token in the sequence, but you produce filler outputs and then keep iterating on these filler outputs. That would be where you really stop on the sequence, where you currently stopped, keep on recurring a bit, and then you move forward.

rubrics.text: The response analogizes recurrent-depth computation to an RNN repeatedly computing at the current sequence position before advancing to the next token.

items.question: What made recurrent depth an interesting approach for you to pursue in language models?
items.object: Recurrent depth for language models
items.answer:
Basically this is all the way back in 2023. Tom and me—Tom is the last author—had just been working on a paper on training language models more efficiently, and then we've been talking a lot about these recurrent models and how they would be cool to do in language, because we really think it would be an interesting language model that could also solve things like math and code better if it could reason more. Back then people were also doing a lot of MoE models, and they're interesting because they're the other extreme: a model that has more parameters but uses less of them. That seems optimal to maybe store information. This is in some conceptual way the opposite: a model that has fewer parameters but uses them over and over and over.

We really wanted to figure out how we could make this paradigm of recurrent depth work with language, how we could modify it, and what a good training objective would be to really scale this up. It really wasn't shown before in transformers at all. From the maze direction, these were always convolutional models, and it wasn't so clear how to put this in a transformer. There was some interesting parallel work on looped transformers, which goes in a related direction, but it didn't quite work as well for us scaling those up larger.

This is also latent: we have a few non-recurrent layers in the model, then this recurrent part in the middle, and then a few more non-recurrent layers at the end. The computation is in this centralized latent space, and there are still layers at the start that decode from language and layers at the end that decode back into language. With the right objective, this helped us a lot.

items.question: How did you experience scaling your recurrent language model from a small prototype to 4,000 GPUs on Frontier?
items.object: Scaling the recurrent language model on Frontier
items.answer:
We had some 100 million parameter prototypes in 2023. Then we teamed up with people who know a lot more about high performance computing and wrote this big allocation grant for ACCESS, some big allocation grant, and got compute at Oak Ridge National Labs.

It was quite an interesting journey. It's one thing to train this model and prototype 100 million parameters, and it's kind of nice to see, okay, now there are 4,000 accelerators and they still have to work together, and this funny little probabilistic objective you wrote still has to scale and work there. That was a pretty interesting journey that I personally enjoyed a lot, although it was a bit harrowing at times, to actually make this work and run this on these cards. This was computed on Frontier, the largest AMD supercomputer in the world. The folks at ACCESS said, “Here, you could have this.”

2024 was also the year where a lot of things were moving at AMD and were just beginning to be supported. For example, FlashAttention is a very basic algorithm for us nowadays, but it took a lot of time, maybe until last July, where I felt this was stable enough that we could reliably deploy it and run it. AMD did a lot, and we had a lot of issues, but we got around them. It did train in the end. It was a whole journey of maybe a year where the underlying little model didn't really change. In the paper, that's section three, 2023, and section four is all of 2024: we trained it on 4,000 GPUs.

Then it got pretty exciting because, as you mentioned, these test-time compute reasoning models came out in fall. We still hadn't finished training the model, and suddenly this was in the news everywhere. We finished training the model in early December last year, which is why we wrote up our results in January and published them. It was a bit of a scary moment as the world caught up to us a bit, although that's also why the approach is a bit different.

items.question: How has your framing of your recurrent language model work as reasoning changed over time?
items.object: The framing of recurrent language model research as reasoning
items.answer: It was always just the idea of reasoning and learning algorithms, but maybe that framing is the more classical framing. These older papers would maybe call this learning an algorithm, or a prior towards learning algorithmic reasoning. To call this all just blanket reasoning maybe that's a more modern way of looking at it. The other part that's also very modern is that in the intro now we clearly call this out: there's verbalized reasoning, which is how we put these other approaches, compared to what we're doing. That's a modern distinction that we put into the claim of what we're doing differently.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between latent reasoning and language-based chain-of-thought reasoning?
items.object: Latent reasoning and language-based chain-of-thought reasoning
items.answer: I really hadn't thought so much that just long chains of thought could scale so well. Maybe this wasn't clear to many of us a year ago. I think it's interesting to look at them in this dichotomy: one is trying to learn these algorithms in a high dimensional space, before it really decodes into language, and the other approach is trying to scaffold reasoning onto language.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between verbalized and nonverbalized reasoning as ways for models to think longer?
items.object: Verbalized and nonverbalized reasoning as complementary ways to extend thinking
items.answer:
Maybe the first thing I think is that this is quite natural for us as well. Maybe really as humans—this is a bit of anthropomorphizing, I hope that's fine—but basically, I think it's clear that we can sometimes think longer about a problem without actually verbalizing the answer in our head. We don't always think steps in our head, especially if it's a problem that maybe relates to spatial reasoning, or something where you have some intuitive motor planning, or planning reasoning, or how you go from one place to another. These are often things that we think about, and we also think about longer, but we don't really verbalize this kind of thinking.

Interestingly, we can still write things down. We can extend our thinking process by verbalizing it, by writing things down in notebooks, in equations. In this way we can externalize thinking and think even longer. Even as humans we have these two ways in which we can scale compute or thinking in this way. It's not necessarily you can do this or the other, but maybe as humans we naturally do both of those, and these models also could do both.

items.question: Why do you see thinking without verbalizing as potentially more powerful for a transformer model?
items.object: Nonverbalized reasoning and the depth limitation of transformers
items.answer: I think what's interesting about thinking without verbalizing it is that from a very basic perspective this just seems much more powerful. The transformer does some calculation because it is N layers deep, let's say 96 layers deep. The model does some calculation and the next word comes out, and then in the next layer it can maybe access these previous calculations, but again only up to the 96th layer. If the model were to do a calculation that's deeper than 96, it's kind of hard because it has to go into these previous attention parts. The model is a bit limited in its depth.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between a transformer's long chain of thought and a recurrent model's handling of hidden representations?
items.object: Hidden representations in transformer chain-of-thought reasoning and recurrent models
items.answer: An interesting analogy to make this clearer is that, if we extract a bit away from it, what the transformer is doing if it's doing a very long chain of thought is that it has some hidden representation that computed on what the next token should be. That whole hidden representation, which is a high dimensional vector, is thrown away, and then one token is sampled out of it. The next step, that token is embedded again to compute a whole other hidden representation, which is thrown away, and then a new token is embedded. We keep embedding and unembedding these representations that the model is providing. Maybe the only thing this recurrent model is doing is that it's not doing that; it's keeping and refining this hidden representation.

items.question: How do you approach deciding when a recurrent language model should stop iterating?
items.object: Adaptive stopping in recurrent language models
items.answer:
Interestingly, that's actually not something we have done a lot in this work. What we've done a lot is show how to scale these models and how to train them to have this capability. The best way we could scale these models was just to train them with a randomized depth, or randomized number of recurrences.

There's some older work called Universal Transformers. This relates to universal Turing completeness, and these models had halting submodules where during training you had to decide when to stop. Those are pretty hard to scale and pretty hard to train, because you're training a model to get better and at the same time training it to exit early. It's hard to bootstrap a model that has to get better on harder problems and has to know when to exit early.

One way we got around this was that during training we have a log-normal distribution, really a heavy-tail distribution, over possible steps, and we sample one of them. We compute loss on this step and backpropagate. At inference time, we found that we could do zero-shot adaptive exits, for example by computing how much the state changes from step to step. We could make a simple rule based on that and exit based on the simple rule that we put in zero-shot afterwards. It was exciting that this actually did work at all.

Those are pretty hard to scale and pretty hard to train, because you're training a model to get better and at the same time training it to exit early. It's hard to bootstrap a model that has to get better on harder problems and has to know when to exit early.

items.question: Why do you find the next-token output distribution a better signal for deciding when a latent recurrent model should stop thinking?
items.object: Output-distribution convergence as a signal for adaptive exits in latent recurrent models
items.answer:
We've tried this with several ones. We've tried this with the actual latent recurrent state, for example the L2 norm of that state to the previous state. We've also done this in the output distribution. At state 16 we compute the next token distribution, then at step 24 we compute the next token distribution again, and compare the KL divergence of these two probability distributions. If that is small, we exit. The idea is that the model's converging on some thought or idea.

Interestingly, the second one seems practically better, because sometimes the model keeps thinking in this recurrent space, and we have some interesting graphics in the paper where we project that down into lower dimensions. This thinking doesn't always reflect in the probability of the next token. A more stable state is actually: what do you predict next?

items.question: What surprised you about how the model's recurrent computation specialized across tokens as it scaled?
items.object: Emergent per-token specialization of recurrence with model scale
items.answer: It wasn't clear to us beforehand whether the model would learn to specialize this recurrence with scale. We have a picture in the paper how the model converges quickly when the next token prediction is easy, but convergence is much slower if the next token prediction is hard, or if it's a token that's somewhat important for understanding the question. We totally didn't train for this. We trained with fixed sequences and assigned them the same step budget for the entire sequence, because that makes sense for pre-training scale. This per-token specialization just seemed to emerge with scale: the model converges quicker on easy tokens than on hard ones. We really didn't know it would work like this before we saw the final model.

items.question: Why did you use the same recurrence step count for every token in a sequence when pretraining your model?
items.object: Uniform recurrence step counts during model pretraining
items.answer: The way the model was pretrained was not only that we picked a random step for every recurrence, but we also picked the same step count for all the tokens in an example sequence. For this to be parallelized, the model has to do the same amount of compute at every token. These sequences are 4,000 tokens long.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between the model’s batch-level training steps and its per-token convergence at test time?
items.object: Batch-level training steps versus per-token convergence at test time
items.answer: We're actually saying, “Okay, this batch gets three steps, this batch gets eight steps, this batch gets 128 steps.” But at test time we see that the model has this convergence graph that's very different on a per-token level. On some tokens it goes green very quickly.

items.question: How do you view the potential for your latent reasoning model to adapt its computation by exiting early on individual tokens?
items.object: Adaptive early exits in the latent reasoning model
items.answer:
In the chart and paper, we run the model for the same number of compute steps for all tokens. That's why this is a rectangular chart. We see how quickly it's done in every token, but to make that chart we actually run all the steps to completion. From that, we imply that you could have exited early.

What I'm really saying is it can do that. For most of the paper we haven't done this a lot yet. We have the section about how you could do adaptive exits and exit early, section 6.3 in the paper, and there we try this. That's where we discover this is possible. A lot of the rest of the paper hasn't caught up to this more adaptive paradigm yet. It's something we were surprised would work at all. I'm personally excited thinking back to these halting modules: now that this model is trained, we can probably fine-tune these stopping modules onto it again, because now the bootstrapping problem is solved. We just haven't gotten to that yet, or no one has, I think.

items.question: What are you trying to achieve by training a recurrent language model with a variable number of compute steps?

items.answer: There have been previous architectures, for example, I'm not sure if you remember something like ALBERT, which was a weight-shared BERT variant. There are also some Universal Transformer models where they have recurrence but the recurrence is always fixed: you always do eight times or 16 times or something. Those models work, but they don't really generalize to fewer or more steps of compute. They train like a fixed-depth transformer, where they lose performance if they go for more steps, and they also don't work if they have fewer steps. With this objective, we try to generalize to really an arbitrary number of steps, so the model is stable and can learn a fixed point or a steady-state behavior. That's what this objective is trying to get it to do.

items.question: How do you understand the idea that a recurrent language model is searching in latent space for the next token?
items.object: Latent-space search and the dynamics of a recurrent language model
items.answer:
It's an interesting way to look at it. In some ways, yes. What's actually happening is that you have some initial state in the recurrence, and the initial state is always random. We can visualize those, and often these random states lie somewhere in the middle if you plot PCA directions, because they don't have a significant component in any direction. As the model recurs, it keeps moving these points away onto some target position where it wants them, and from there it can predict the next token.

We have these funny little spine charts in the end of the paper where you see this middle column rising, and then you have these trajectories going out at the end. I think it's somewhere in the appendix where you see that from random it converges to, or finds, this point from which to predict the next token.

What's also super exciting for us is that this is not always just a point. It doesn't always just converge to a fixed point. We also observe the model rotating; it has these little orbits that it makes. It's still very hard for me to visualize this 5,280-dimensional space, so I can only show the first 40 or 80 PCA directions. In those we can see trajectories that come together and then do these little circles. In later tokens it can pick up on these circles or orbits it had done in earlier steps and do some calculation with that. We know models often implement additional algorithms with these sorts of schemes, where you have orbits that reinforce each other. It was quite interesting because it really was an emerging behavior.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between your recurrent latent reasoning model and diffusion models?
items.object: The relationship between recurrent latent reasoning and diffusion models
items.answer:
From some perspective, this really is a diffusion model. Maybe that's a bit generic, because all recurrent models are, or maybe both of them are recurrent models. Diffusion models are also recurrent models in a different way. It's important to separate that from the exciting language diffusion models recently. If you think about this as a diffusion model, you pick one token, the next token, and then you diffuse all the way until you found the next token. Then you go one step forward and diffuse again until you found the next token, and go one step forward and diffuse again.

During development we tried to make this a bit more explicit. We tried not only to start from a noisy state, but also to inject noise proportional to how many states, how many steps, you'd done so far, like you would in a diffusion model. This didn't really help during pretraining, so we removed that part again. It shows this analogy that this recurrence is not so different from a diffusion model that would diffuse the next token.

What's quite different is that the objective, the training objective, is very different. Ideally in a diffusion model you would want a process where you have a continuous target and add some noise to it, and then learn this denoising operation. That's how large-scale image diffusion models are trained. In language that's not so clear, because you can try to do noise embeddings, but it's not so nice to do that there. The training objective here is still quite different from a diffusion model.

items.question: How did you navigate the practical challenges of scaling your model from 100 million to 3.5 billion parameters with the supercomputer allocation you had?
items.object: Scaling model training under a constrained supercomputer allocation
items.answer:
What was kind of tough about this was that ultimately this was pretty much a one-shot, because we had a limited amount of compute on the supercomputer, which we also had in little segments. You apply for it in a queuing system, and then you get some 12-hour slot sometime in the year or sometime in the month, and you kind of hope that it's running when it's running.

We only had these little 100 million parameter test models where lots of things worked, and then we were saying, “Okay, now we're scaling it up.” There were some first questions: what's the data parallel strategy, what's the model parallelism strategy? It was a bit harrowing. It was on AMD GPUs, so we had issues, and the cluster wasn't supposed to be running deep learning workloads on more than 128 nodes. The interconnect between the nodes wasn't quite stable, but we had this allocation for 512 nodes, 4,000 cards. These are the MI250X cards, the AMD equivalent of the A100s, older generation cards, so you need more of those to get a similar number of flops as a few more modern cards.

The cluster wasn't really set up to do this kind of thing. We ended up cooking this distributed data parallel pipeline that we pretty much hand-wrote. It only worked if you sent packages that are exactly 64 megabytes over the interconnect. That ended up working and was stable, and it works for no other node count than 512 in this training script. Ultimately we threw out PyTorch DDP and wrote our own funny little version that only sends these 64-megabyte packages, because that was somehow optimal to not overwhelm the interconnect on these machines. This was a whole side quest that took us several months to figure out how to actually run with this allocation. We're academics, we're pretty happy about any compute we have, and we can make it work, but it could take us some time to make it work.

items.question: Why did you choose to train your recurrent latent-reasoning model from scratch?
items.object: Training a recurrent latent-reasoning model from scratch versus retrofitting a fixed-depth transformer
items.answer: Because this approach is so different, it really had to be trained from scratch to do this. They try to get that from retrofitting fixed-depth transformers, which is interesting, especially for companies: if you already have your large fixed-depth transformer, can you retrofit this capability into it? For us, we really wanted to see, can we train from the ground up for this model to be recurrent and do more compute for hard problems?

items.question: How do you think about comparing your recurrent 3.5-billion-parameter model to a 50-billion-parameter model?
items.object: The comparison between the recurrent 3.5-billion-parameter model and a 50-billion-parameter model
items.answer: A good way to think about the model is that it actually only has eight layers: two layers before the recurrence, four layers in the recurrence that are being repeated, and then two layers at the end that produce the final next token. This whole thing is just 3.5 billion parameters, but if we run it for more steps, say 32 steps, we run the middle part much longer. It would be as if we had run it for something like 50 billion parameters. We still have only 3.5 billion. The actual calculation is that we have 1.5 billion fixed parameters and 1.5 billion recurrent parameters, so in compute it takes as much time to get the next answer as if it was a 50 billion parameter model, but it's still a tiny 3.5 billion parameter model. It's not a 50 billion parameter model in comparison. It's not like it's a Llama 70B model; it's not nearly as good, because ultimately it's trained for much less compute.

items.question: What do you take away from your recurrent model's benchmark performance relative to the OLMo series?
items.object: The recurrent model's benchmark performance relative to the OLMo series
items.answer: In benchmarks it's quite good. It compares to other open-source models like the OLMo series. We were very happy that we could catch up to the OLMo v1 models and v1.5. That was exciting because those models were trained by a much larger, much more capable team. We're just a bunch of guys in the basement. items.question: Do you think parameter count is becoming less useful for comparing language models as their architectures incorporate more reasoning compute?
items.object: Parameter count as a way to compare language models
items.answer:
I think so. For us, even this was already super tough to compare in parameters. The model is actually smaller than all the other ones we compared to, but in compute, for some of the benchmarks, how do we compare this if the model is smaller but we spend more compute on getting the answer compared to these larger models that spend less compute? The same thing happens with other reasoning models. For example, the R1 model may be 64 billion active parameters, but do you count it as a 64 billion parameter active model, or a thousand tokens of chain of thought times 64 billion active parameters? It's not so clear how to do this calculation. It becomes somehow less meaningful.

One thing we can do is convert pretraining FLOPs to what model size we could have trained with that compute budget. That comes up to something like a 32 billion parameter model in raw FLOPs, so not small for a similar token count. Interestingly, we couldn't have trained a 32 billion parameter normal transformer on this node setup, because this model is so much smaller and so much more communication efficient. There is less state to send to the other devices.

items.question: What do you find striking about the reasoning performance of your recurrent language model?
items.object: The recurrent language model’s reasoning performance
items.answer:
Our model is surprisingly good at reasoning. In the benchmarks, especially on grade-school math—not graduate math, grade-school math. Tiny, tiny, big difference. GSM8K is a classical grade-school math problem. Also on HumanEval, which is the coding—these are nowadays easy coding questions—the model is particularly good, and it is actually better than some of the other open-source models by the other teams.

What's particularly exciting is that, while we had limited compute, we did train a baseline comparison model where we trained the exact same architecture, the exact same data, the exact same cluster, but trained it to always have a recurrence of one. That would be a fixed-depth comparison. The model has the same number of parameters and we trained it just the same way. We trained that one for 10,000 steps, which is about 180 billion tokens. Interestingly that fixed-depth version got a GSM8K score of 1.5% or something, and at 180 billion tokens the recurrent model already was at 10 to 12% of GSM8K, five times better at grade-school math. Same number of parameters, just a different way of using them, and it was drastically better at grade-school math. The comparison is hard, but we haven't trained the baseline all the way to the end, so some of these comparisons are hard because ultimately we have this one data point.

items.question: Why do you see recurrent depth as a practical way to use transformers?
items.object: The practicality of recurrent-depth transformer architectures
items.answer:
What we really want to show in this section is that this is a very natural way to use transformers. Leaving all the thinking and reasoning and loftier motivations aside, we think it's also a practical architecture. There are several examples in that section about why it's practical.

We've talked about these adaptive exits already. This is something you can also do in a normal transformer. People have tried it: if you have 96 layers, maybe on some tokens you only use the first eight or something. Then they get into, how do you fine-tune for this, how do you make this happen? It's a big effort to fine-tune the model for that. We show that this different architecture can just do a zero-shot exit.

Something similar holds for things like speculative decoding.

items.question: What do you find interesting about using a recurrent transformer architecture for speculative decoding?
items.object: Speculative decoding with a recurrent transformer architecture
items.answer: To recap that slightly, for speculative decoding ideally you need this little draft model, and it kind of needs to be aligned with the large model, and it needs to fit, and you need to really make that work and do some engineering. There was a lot of good research being done to make that work. What I find kind of interesting about this recurrent architecture is that just naturally, by running it for one step or four steps, you have your own draft model in your back pocket. You can run the model for a small number of steps to draft, and then still verify with 64 steps. It just happens like that: no fine-tuning necessary, no draft model making necessary. It just fits like that.

items.question: How do you understand the advantage of a recurrent transformer architecture for sharing KV caches?
items.object: KV cache sharing in recurrent transformers
items.answer: There's also this idea that you'd want to do KV cache sharing, where you have several layers that share the same KV cache so you can push down in the KV cache. In normal transformers that's a bit hard because all the layers have different K and V projection matrices, so the KV caches don't really match each other. But this model, because it's just a recurrence and always the same parameters are being used, can naturally share KV caches between steps if I wanted to.

items.question: How do you view the memory-efficiency advantages of reusing parameters in your recurrent model during inference?
items.object: Memory efficiency and parameter reuse in recurrent model architectures
items.answer:
The model is much smaller. You can run it on a smaller chip and run it longer on the smaller chip. We kind of wanted it—or maybe not wanted it—but a different thing you could want is that the entire recurrence fits into an L1 cache. It's a bit too large for that, but if it would, it would be even faster. Right now you still have about a billion parameters in the recurrence that you keep moving out of the L2 into the L1, so there's still some movement there. Overall, you need much less memory on the device to actually store the model, which we think is exciting for some low-resource applications and for having fewer parameters around instead of these massive models where we use every parameter only once and then throw it away.

It's quite an interesting paradigm that we try to reuse parameters. There are other ways to use this in interesting ways that we just haven't figured out yet. These are some examples in the section that I thought were pretty interesting. It's a different architecture; it has these different advantages that we weren't maybe so aware of, even putting all the reasoning aside. This might just be more efficient in some applications.

items.question: What do you find interesting about including instruction data and chat templates during your model's pretraining?
items.object: Including instruction data and chat templates during model pretraining
items.answer: What's interesting—and this is a funny quirk—is that we actually trained the model with instruction data, with chat templates in the pretraining. Some other people have also done that; it's a bit more rare. We did this because we didn't have compute for a longer post-training or cooldown phase. What it implies is that the model learns the chat template from the get-go. You can chat with all these intermediate checkpoints already, which is kind of a fun thing. You can chat with the 10,000-step state of the model and see how it's doing and how it's understanding some questions, and you can also chat with the later ones. It inherently understands this chat template format.

items.question: Why do you think a language model reasoning in latent states poses no worse a safety problem than one producing a textual chain of thought?
items.object: Latent reasoning versus text-based chain of thought and model safety
items.answer:
I think the first answer, why I think this is not worse, which I also talked with colleagues about, is that I already didn't think that language models think in text. For me this was a very small step, because if you think about it, if you have a very long chain of thought, the model takes these text intermediate steps as text inputs, but mostly the model attends to its own internal representations of these previous tokens. If you think about the attention and all the layers, you're already attending to these very deep representations of these tokens, and you sort of already don't know what's in these states. Text is a reflection of some opaque latent space anyway.

The thinking isn't really happening in text; it's happening in that domain. The model is prompted with a new token and incorporates that into its hidden states, but it already thinks based on its previous hidden states. With this model, maybe this is just a bit more explicit.

items.question: How do you think research on your latent reasoning model should balance developing its capabilities with understanding how it works?
items.object: Future research on the latent reasoning model
items.answer:
Yeah, it's really both of the above. The most immediate thing is that the model actually isn't even cooled down, just because we don't have any compute anymore. That's the very real answer why it didn't cool down.

For the later models, we see the models improve a lot with this mid-training phase where the model is slowly cooled down from its peak learning rate to a zero learning rate using a very high-quality data mix. For me, the first thing on the agenda is to try some data mixes, maybe tailor more towards code, more towards math, and see what these cooldown behaviors look like for this kind of model. That's already interesting, because you could also play around with the parameters. You could imagine that you could cool down with more steps than you did during pretraining, so you could incentivize it to think deeper during the cooldown phase.

There are also other questions we have on the team, like how would you even post-train this kind of model? How would you do it? These are questions in the room, aside from questions of what is it doing internally, how can we understand it, how can we probe it?
